Security review: BLOCK (round 1)
PR: #237
Head: 81f4a89974383caf7dd5bf727f3f468c0d389ed2
Request: 01a1ec54-4584-7ca2-ac59-a8e4c0f2bc60

S237-001 | MEDIUM | confidence 9/10
crates/daemon/src/http/identity.rs:616-624

Explicit takeover bypasses the live-holder refusal. After the pane-own-process
authorization at identity.rs:578-585, takeover tombstones the other matching
records without checking their process liveness. The filter's is_live means
not already tombstoned, not that the recorded process is dead or unknown.
The compare-and-swap guards against a changed record, not an unchanged holder
whose process is still running.

Retirement drops pending FYIs (crates/store/src/registry.rs:80-90) and releases
open number claims (lines 91-94); released numbers remain burned.

Normal-use case: while an omp -p child still runs in its parent's pane, the
parent's authorized adopt --take-over can retire that child's live seat.
This violates the requested live-holder guard even under C33's same-user
trust boundary; no hostile local caller or per-seat isolation is assumed.

Reject confirmed-live foreign holders before any takeover retirement, preserve
the explicit unknown-holder recovery path, and add a focused regression for
an authorized non-prime caller against a process-live foreign holder.
Assert that the holder and its pending work remain unchanged on refusal.
The existing takeover test at identity_tests.rs:1927 supplies dead/unbound
holders; the active-holder refusal coverage tests automatic registration,
not the explicit takeover path.

S237-002 | MEDIUM | confidence 9/10
crates/daemon/src/http/identity.rs:567-579

The prime bypass uses a self-asserted seat role, not authoritative project or
orchestration designation. A resolved caller with stored role "prime" is
authorized before the target-pane process-ancestry check. An ordinary seat
may assign that role to itself (http/role.rs:180-202,528-545); "prime" is valid
(crates/core/src/orchestration/governance.rs:160-172). RoleService reads
seat_roles, not a prime designation (http/role.rs:238-243;
crates/store/src/orchestration.rs:311-319).

Consequently, a non-designated seat can self-assign the display/assertion role
and then take over an unrelated pane. The new test self-assigns that role and
expects unrelated-pane takeover success (identity_tests.rs:2004-2016), so it
pins the wrong authority. This conflicts with the role/designation distinction
in skills/pij/references/routes/node.md:18 and the packet's requirement that an
unrelated seat cannot reach the prime path without being the prime.

The predicate is inherited from --reclaim, but the capability is broader:
reclaim additionally requires matching harness and refuses active holders and
live rows without process evidence (identity.rs:506-548); takeover's retirement
at lines 616-624 lacks those restrictions. The new destructive scope is not
proved safe merely by reusing the old authority predicate.

Use the applicable authoritative prime designation for the bypass, retaining
caller derivation and contradictory-claim refusals. Add a focused regression
showing that a self-asserted, non-designated prime cannot take over an unrelated
pane, while the actual designated prime can. This is a cheap authority/correctness
guard under C33, not a claim that same-user processes require OS or per-seat
security isolation.

Evidence and limits:
- Exact checkout and GitHub head agree; worktree is clean.
- No prior outputs or GitHub reviews were present for this PR: first round.
- CI run 44217294613 is for this exact head.
- Successful rust-test job 134510197257: 2438 passed, 6 skipped.
- Exact JUnit artifact 14388744100 was selected from that successful job's
  upload log. All five Rust tests named in the PR body passed.
- Node 22 job 134510197705: native tests 355 passed, 0 failed, including
  the F196 typed-refusal/banner regression. Its sole failed step is the
  audit gate reporting GHSA-fc5q-39xc-vjpf (picomatch).
- Node 24 job 134510197496: npm test passed; native-test step was cancelled.
- rust-lint and delivers passed.
- just pr-freeze 237 exited 1: NOT FINAL because merge is BLOCKED and the
  failed/cancelled checks are not green. The source-security block above is
  independent of that CI status. #236 is still open and addresses the audit
  exception separately; this review does not certify it.
- Read-only source/CI review only. No local cargo build/test, dependency
  installation, mutation run, harness boot or harness checks was performed,
  per the review packet. CI is Linux; macOS behavior has static proof only.
- This is the completed round-1 source review of the same requested head, not
  a review of fixes or a new round-2 finding.

Policy/brake: automatic supersession's confirmed-dead/recycled decision is
policy; uncertain probes are a brake and must not automatically retire rows.
The finding concerns explicit takeover's missing live-holder brake.

Other source coverage: automatic unknown handling refuses missing/invalid
process tuples, remote holders and failed probes (registration.rs:676-686);
ownership is rechecked under lock (registration.rs:853,875-887,1728-1736).
Explicit takeover uses transactional descriptor CAS (registry.rs:61-75).
The macOS lsof endpoint correlation and /bin/ps ancestry were read by eye
(identity.rs:647-700). The banner validates pane/holder fields and rebuilds
the command rather than using remote command text
(.copilot/extensions/pij/store.mjs:721-730,773-774). Tombstoning records actor
and reason without signalling/killing a process (identity.rs:619-624).

Non-blocking command-help note, not another security vulnerability:
registration.rs:51 and store.mjs:774 print an unquoted --why <reason>
placeholder. This does not inject remote text, but it is not shell-runnable;
quote the example reason as requested. Added tests cover missing/remote holders,
not an actual failed-probe result; that extra fixture is optional hardening.

Harness feedback: the successful takeover test lacks a process-live foreign
holder and its prime test uses assertion instead of designation. Encode these
normal-use guards as regressions so successful authorization cannot be mistaken
for proof of safe retirement.
